# 2. The Sharing–Sparing Axis {#sec-sharing-sparing}

The axis answers one question about a site: **what happened to agricultural production on this ground?** Five positions, **S1** through **S5**, run from production continuing inside the array footprint to production ending on ground that was carrying a burden off-site. Every project on land occupies exactly one of them. This is the second of the two dimensions, and it runs largely free of [scale](1-the-scale-transect.qmd), so a barnyard array and a regional complex can sit at the same position. Scale tells you what a project was *able* to do before anyone started designing; this tells you what it actually did with the land.

Most public argument about solar on farmland is an argument about this axis, conducted without it [@moore2022]. Roughly half of the ~3,000 km² (740,000 acres) of US ground-mounted solar was built on former cropland, and about a third on agricultural grassland [@kruitwagen2021; @fujita2023]. *We are losing farmland. It's dual use. That ground was never any good anyway. The lease is what keeps us farming.* Those are four claims about four different positions, and each of the terms in circulation, including dual use, marginal land, and farmland loss, smuggles in a position without naming one. Fixing the position first settles what a project may fairly claim, what it still has to argue for, and which objections actually apply to it. A site's position also outlasts the owner, the power buyer, and the seed mix, which is why it is worth writing down carefully.

The framing comes from a long-running argument in conservation ecology [@green2005; @phalan2011]: is it better to farm gently everywhere, or to farm hard in some places and leave others alone entirely? That question is genuinely unsettled, which is what makes it useful here. The axis takes the same neutrality, describing a real choice without ranking it, so no position is better than another by definition. The closest existing scheme for solar landscapes sorts projects by how ambitious the design is, as mixed-production, nature-based, or landscape-inclusive [@oudes2022]. This axis cuts across all three, because it only asks what happened to production.

### 2.1 The positions {#sec-positions}

::: {.position-table}
| Position | Description | Characteristic |
|---|---|---|
| **S1 — Full sharing** | Production continues within the array footprint, in the same ground | Vegetable [agrivoltaics](5-terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics); crops between rows |
| **S2 — Functional sharing** | Ground layer is productive but subordinate to the array; grazing, forage | Solar grazing at any scale |
| **S3 — Coexistence** | *Neither sharing nor sparing.* The array takes ordinary ground outright, production stops on it, and the revenue sustains the farm enterprise that holds it. Land and farm coexist at the level of the business rather than the field | The lease that keeps a working farm solvent and in operation |
| **S4 — Idled-land sparing** | Array occupies ground already idle, marginal, or out of production, so that productive land is spared | Awkward remnants, fallow ground, brightfields |
| **S5 — Impaired-land retirement** | Production ends on ground that carried a measurable off-site burden, such as chronically low yields, high runoff, nutrient or pesticide export, or irrigation draw beyond the aquifer's budget, or on ground positioned where that burden can be intercepted | Prairie strips on runoff-prone ground; retiring drainage-impaired irrigated fields |
:::

The center of the axis is coexistence, and it is where most projects sit. Crops grown directly underneath or between panels account for only a small share of what has been built, on the order of 2% of US installations [@stid2022; @macknick2022], so full sharing is the exception and a design vocabulary for solar on farmland cannot stop at agrivoltaics. An ordinary array on ordinary ground produces no co-yield and retires no ground; that field becomes a power plant. What can still be restorative about it is the farm. Where the lease is the margin that keeps an operation from being sold, funding the succession, retiring the debt, or carrying the farm through a bad decade, the project restores the enterprise even though it restores nothing in the soil. That is the [community & economic function](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community) (§4.5) doing its work, and **S3 is therefore the position where restoration is socioeconomic before it is biophysical**.

Coexistence is not simply "solar on farmland." It requires that the arrangement sustain the farm enterprise holding the ground, and that test has a precedent. @stid2025 define agrisolar *security* as a farmer's capacity to maintain or improve their financial well-being, operational resilience, and access to essential resources while preserving the integrity and future of their agricultural practices, and they find that commercial-scale landowners in California's Central Valley gained financial security worth roughly 25 times the food revenue they gave up over an array's lifetime. Where the same conversion returns rent to a non-farming owner and the operation ends, the site is **bare conversion**, the identical ground fact without the restorative one. The field already has a name for that case, since replacing agricultural land with solar without agrivoltaic management "has historically been considered *conventional solar*" and excluded from co-location research altogether [@stid2025]. Bare conversion is the baseline the axis is read against rather than a position on it. Which farm, and whose, is a real question: a lease can sustain a landowner and end a tenant's operation at the same time, so the test is applied to the actors set out in §4.5.

The sparing wing splits on what the ground was doing beforehand. S4 and S5 both end production, but they are different acts, and the difference is where the benefit lands. S4 takes ground that had already stopped paying, sending the array to the awkward corner precisely so the good field is left alone, and the benefit accrues to *the land not taken*. S5 ends production on ground that was exporting a burden, so it acts on *the ground taken itself*, and on the water leaving it. A flood-prone corner planted to solar spares the field next to it; a drainage-impaired field retired under prairie and panels stops sending nitrogen downstream, the documented effect of prairie plantings in corn–soybean cropland [@schulte2017]. Both are removal, but only one changes what the ground was doing to everyone else.

A position records the ground fact, not the quality of the project. Two S3 sites can differ completely, one carrying gravel and herbicide and the other a native planting rich in pollinators, and they hold the same position because the same thing happened to production. What separates them is the [restorative functions](4-restorative-functions.qmd) layered on top. Ecological ground layers live there rather than on this axis: pollinator habitat, prairie, and native grassland are functions (§4) reachable from S2 through S5, so native grassland under a utility array is S3 carrying a biodiversity function, and the same planting on retired leaching ground is S5 carrying it. The axis says what happened to the production; §4 says what the land was made to do. Reading benefit straight off a position is the error §4 names as the [category correction](4-restorative-functions.qmd).

The positions are exclusive, and two questions in order settle which one applies.

1. **Does agricultural production continue within the footprint?** If it does, the site is **S1** (production in the same ground) or **S2** (a productive but subordinate ground layer), whatever the ground used to be. A flood-prone corner that still carries the farm's sheep is S2, not S4.
2. **If production has stopped, what was the ground beforehand?** Ordinary productive land gives **S3**, ground already idle or marginal gives **S4**, and ground carrying a measurable off-site burden gives **S5**. The same flood-prone corner, left to naturalize under the panels, is S4.

S3 asks one further question, which is whether the farm enterprise survives the conversion. Where it does not, the site is bare conversion rather than S3.

Two boundaries are worth stating plainly. S4 holds unlike things together: idled cropland, awkward remnants, reclaimed mine land, landfills, and brownfields share the one fact that the ground was already out of production, but they differ in prior use, contamination, permitting path, remediation constraints on foundations and ground layer, and in what the community reads the reuse as meaning. The position records the shared fact, and those differences belong to the site description. Arrays on buildings, meanwhile, hold no position at all, because a built surface has no prior land status. That is the [A0 zero-land case](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) (§1.2), at the transect's origin. The axis is defined over ground, and where there is no ground there is no position.

### 2.2 Which positions scale allows {#sec-wedge}

The two dimensions are independent in principle but not fully in practice, and the constraint runs through [siting latitude](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) (§1.4). A position is not simply chosen. Scale narrows the menu before the design meeting starts, and knowing which positions are realistically open at your scale is most of the value of reading the two dimensions together.

Both sparing positions assume somebody who gets to pick which acres to take. At A4–A5, where siting is governed by assembling contiguous land near a substation, that freedom is largely gone, because a five-hundred-acre block contains good and poor ground mixed together. Large projects are pushed toward the S2–S3 middle by structural necessity rather than preference: if you cannot choose *which* ground, the remaining options are to do something worthwhile with all of it, or nothing with any of it.

The two sparing positions then behave differently at scale. S4 thins for a geometric reason, since idle remnants are scattered and assembling a utility-scale project out of flood-prone corners is impractical where it is possible at all. S5 survives at scale wherever the impairment is regional rather than scattered, as in a drainage-impaired valley or a district over its groundwater budget. Where a whole landscape is impaired, retirement and scale stop fighting each other because there is no cherry-picking to do. This is an expectation drawn from the archetypes rather than a measured result.

Read the axis from its center. **S3 sits on the scale line**, with full and functional sharing (S1–S2) above it and the two removal positions (S4–S5) below. The feasible region is then not a rectangle but a lens, the *feasible wedge*, widest at A3 (Parcel) and closing toward the S2–S3 middle at both extremes of scale. It closes for different reasons at each end, and neither end is a hard wall.

![The feasible region as a lens on a centred five-position axis, widest at A3 (Parcel) and closing toward the S2–S3 middle at both extremes of scale. Grazing (S2) and coexistence (S3) run the spine at every scale. Solid points are exemplar practices; hollow points are exceptions that reopen a thinned corner. Hatching marks where the space thins, lightly at small scale (feasible but atypical or negligible) and densely at large scale (strongly constrained).](../figures/fig_feasible_wedge.svg){#fig-wedge}

Four things follow. Grazing and coexistence are the spine, since functional sharing is genuinely available at every scale, from a farmer's own flock at A1 through a contracted service at A3 to a multi-site rotation enterprise at A5 (§1.3), and coexistence is available everywhere for the opposite reason: it asks nothing of the ground. Both extremes then converge on that middle. At A5 siting is dictated by land assembly, so sparing loses the freedom to choose its ground, and tight budgets make full sharing's tall clearances and wide rows hard to justify; at A1 the narrowing is gentler, because no one farms *under* a two-panel array and a spared idle corner is real but too small to matter.

The thinned corners are not walls. Small-scale full sharing returns where the structure is purpose-built to farm under, as in greenhouse photovoltaics. Utility-scale full sharing returns with vertical bifacial arrays, whose open inter-rows relax the clearance constraint [@vaverkova2026]. Utility-scale S4 returns on uniformly low-value pre-disturbed land, meaning reclaimed mine land, landfills, and brightfields, where sparing and scale coexist without cherry-picking acres. Utility-scale S5 returns wherever impairment is regional, which is the exception with the most land behind it. All five positions are genuinely open at A3, which is why so many of the most interesting projects to learn from are that size.

*Native grassland is plotted at S3 because that is where it is most often built, not because it is a position. It is a [restorative function](4-restorative-functions.qmd) reachable across the axis, and at utility scale it carries documented biodiversity and soil-carbon gains [@walston2025; @krasner2025].*

S1 is not equally attractive everywhere. In-footprint crop benefit is strongly climate- and crop-conditional, pronounced in water-limited, high-radiation settings and for shade-tolerant crops [@barrongafford2019], but mixed to net-negative for staple grains and in temperate or humid settings where shade costs yield without a compensating water saving [@weselek2019]. Full sharing is a regional proposition rather than a universal one.

*The clearest counterexample to the reading above would be a utility-scale S4 project assembled from scattered marginal remnants on ordinary farmland, rather than from the uniform pre-disturbed ground the standing exception already allows. None is documented here, and one would be worth reporting.*

American Farmland Trust holds that [dual use](5-terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics) means active farming continuing inside the array footprint for the project's whole 30–40 year life. Put on this axis, that is a requirement to be at S1 or S2. Critics argue that it marginalizes ecovoltaics, whose ecological ground layers deliver their value as a function rather than as production [@hernandez2019], and so sit at S3 and below. Stated as positions, the disagreement becomes tractable: it is a dispute about which stretch of the axis deserves the name, not about what the word means. This document describes that dispute rather than settling it. *(See §5, Agrivoltaics / Ecovoltaics.)*

### Terms

Terms introduced in this section are defined in the [Terminology](5-terminology.qmd) chapter (§5), under [Sharing and sparing](5-terminology.qmd#sec-terms-sharing), alongside every other term the document defines.
